extracted.intended_audience: general readers, TV viewers, media researchers interested in The Daily Show and its international distribution/spin-offs
extracted.subtask_description: A Wikipedia-style encyclopedic article describing The Daily Show: its international broadcasts, edits/censorship, format choices, spin-offs, and related distribution practices. Focuses on how the program is packaged and adapted for different regions and platforms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Syndication edits (content/language/length/commercial references)
rubrics_metrics.description: Broadcasters (e.g., More4) that syndicated entire episodes sometimes made edits to the program due to content, language, length or commercial references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: More4 was the first international broadcaster to syndicate entire Daily Show episodes but still edited material for the above reasons. This implies that international syndication often requires trimming or modifying segments to meet local broadcast standards or time/format constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of commercial breaks (British format)
rubrics_metrics.description: Placement of commercial breaks followed the British format, with one break midway through the show rather than several short breaks at various points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a formatting/scheduling choice affecting episode structure for certain international broadcasts; producers and syndicators should plan segment lengths and pacing to accommodate a single mid-show break when airing in markets that prefer the British format.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parliamentary/procedural broadcasting rules (UK)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliamentary rules ban parliamentary proceedings from being broadcast in a satirical context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequence/example: The Global Edition for the week of July 20, 2011, was not aired in the UK because it included a segment mocking Rupert Murdoch's appearance before the House of Commons committee. Producers and distributors must respect jurisdictional rules about using parliamentary footage or proceedings in satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regional scheduling / airing delay conventions
rubrics_metrics.description: International channels sometimes schedule episodes on a delay (e.g., episodes shown 24 hours after U.S. airing) or on specific weekdays (e.g., More4 airing on Mondays; regular episodes airing the evening following American airing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Comedy Central Extra announced episodes would be shown 24 hours after U.S. airing. Syndicators should coordinate timing expectations and communicate delays to viewers; scheduling affects relevance for topical satire.

rubrics_metrics.name: Online availability varies by country
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodes of the American version are made available online (often the next day) on Comedy Central's official Daily Show website, but this service is not available in all countries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Clips for UK and Ireland became available on the UK Comedy Central website in December 2011; Australian episodes were available on ABC iView shortly after airing until rights changed. Digital distribution rights and geoblocking vary by territory and may limit international viewers' access to full episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Localization for international editions / adaptation to local news
rubrics_metrics.description: Official international editions (e.g., The Daily Show: Nederlandse Editie) are similar in format to the original but replace U.S.-centric material with domestic news and a local view on international events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The Dutch edition used Dutch news and perspectives and featured a local host. Guidance: spin-offs should retain the satirical-news format while adapting content, references, and comedic voice to the local audience; local relevance is essential for viewership (the Dutch test run ended after 12 episodes due to lack of viewers).

rubrics_metrics.name: Editing for regional appropriateness / censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodes are often edited if they contain topics deemed inappropriate for the region, and some episodes or segments may be withheld entirely for censorship or regulatory reasons.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Global Edition not aired in the UK for certain segments; episodes may be shortened or cut for content/language. Distributors and producers must anticipate regional sensitivities and legal/regulatory limits when shipping content internationally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hiatus programming practice
rubrics_metrics.description: When The Daily Show was on hiatus, broadcasters typically aired re-runs or alternative content in its place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Programmers should plan replacement content for hiatus periods; syndicators rely on reruns/alternatives to maintain schedule slots and viewer retention during host or production breaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Companion digital/audio content strategy (podcasts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Companion podcasts (e.g., The Daily Show: Ears Edition) are used as extended-format companions to the main television program, offering extended information and additional interviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The Ears Edition replaced an earlier podcast and served as a companion piece; producers can use podcast mini-series to expand reach, provide deeper interviews, or preserve audience engagement between television episodes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spin-off development/testing practice (pilotless trial run)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spin-offs have sometimes been developed and trialed without producing a traditional pilot (e.g., The Colbert Report was agreed to run for eight weeks without first creating a pilot).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Colbert, Stewart, and Ben Karlin pitched the idea and Comedy Central agreed to run it for eight weeks; initial ratings and reception then informed renewal decisions. This suggests networks may accept short-run real-air testing instead of conventional pilot production for proven talent/brands.
